key_insight: Snoring acoustics alone can help distinguish palatal from epiglottic upper-airway obstruction in obstructive sleep apnea, suggesting a non-invasive acoustic phenotype.
clinical_relevance: If validated further, this approach could support lower-burden, more scalable screening or anatomical assessment compared with invasive DISE.
method: Retrospective analysis of 159 DISE recordings from adults with moderate, non-positional OSA
Expert examiners labeled snoring events by anatomical source; only fully agreed events were kept
Extracted spectral, cepstral, temporal, and harmonic features and trained SVM/MLP models with nested patient-independent cross-validation
evidence_signal: Using 1,759 snoring events (1,054 palatal; 705 epiglottic), both models achieved ROC AUC 0.90 ± 0.03 with balanced accuracy around 0.81–0.83 under patient-independent validation.
watch_item: This is a retrospective, single-dataset study based on DISE-labeled events, so generalizability to broader patients and real-world recording conditions still needs prospective validation.
paper_title: The sound of snoring: AI-based acoustic phenotyping of upper airway obstruction in Obstructive Sleep Apnea
